rows: Slurry storage should be designed and maintained to prevent water pollution.
Stores should have sufficient capacity for required storage periods and foreseeable rainfall.
Walls, floors, channels and tanks should be impermeable and structurally sound.
Safety zones and separation from watercourses apply to relevant structures.
Drainage should prevent clean water unnecessarily entering the store.
Stores and associated equipment should be inspected and maintained.
New or substantially enlarged stores require advance Environment Agency notification where applicable.
Leaks, overflows or structural defects require prompt control and reporting.
A calculated capacity or recent inspection does not prove that a slurry store is compliant and safe.
Conclusions require dimensions, rainfall allowance, contents, structure, drainage, separation, notification, inspection and operating evidence.
Silage effluent is highly polluting and must be collected and contained.
Silage stores should have impermeable floors and suitable drainage.
Effluent channels and tanks should be resistant to corrosion and leakage.
Stores should be located with required separation from watercourses and drainage systems.
Capacity should reflect the silage type and likely effluent production.
Structures and collection systems should be inspected and maintained.
New or substantially enlarged facilities require advance notification where applicable.
Leaks or uncontrolled effluent should trigger immediate pollution-response action.
A clamp design or empty effluent tank does not prove that silage pollution risk is controlled.
Conclusions require crop, store, floor, channels, tank capacity, separation, condition, notification and operating evidence.
The Yellow Card scheme supports MHRA monitoring of the safety of medicines and healthcare products.
Patients, healthcare professionals and other reporters can submit suspected adverse reactions.
Only a suspicion of an adverse drug reaction is needed to make a report.
Serious suspected reactions to established medicines and vaccines should be reported.
All suspected reactions to products under additional black-triangle monitoring should be reported.
Reports can also cover medical-device incidents and defective or counterfeit products.
Useful reports include product details, reaction description, timing and relevant medical information.
MHRA reviews reports with other evidence and can take action to reduce risk.
A Yellow Card report does not prove that the product caused the reported event.
Conclusions require case details, exposure, timing, alternative causes, clinical evidence, reporting context and wider safety data.
MHRA is the regulatory authority for medical devices placed on the UK market.
Manufacturers must report qualifying UK device incidents under the vigilance system.
Reportability depends on the event, device involvement and actual or potential serious outcome.
Field safety corrective actions form part of the vigilance system.
Manufacturers should investigate incidents and assess device risk.
Post-market information should be reviewed for trends and recurring failures.
Reports should contain sufficient device, event and patient or user information.
Corrective and preventive actions should be implemented and monitored where required.
A complaint, malfunction or single injury does not automatically determine regulatory reportability or causation.
Conclusions require device identity, event sequence, outcome, recurrence, investigation, risk assessment, reporting criteria and corrective-action evidence.
